oneLineAnswer: Capecitabine is an oral chemotherapy tablet that your body turns into fluorouracil to slow cancer growth.
whatItIs: Capecitabine is a prescription chemotherapy medicine taken as tablets you swallow. It is a prodrug, which means your body changes it into the active drug, fluorouracil. The drug label calls it a nucleoside metabolic inhibitor. That means it interferes with how cells build DNA and RNA. Its brand name is Xeloda. In chemistry terms it has the formula C15H22FN3O6 and a molecular weight of 359.35. Tablets come in 150 mg and 500 mg strengths.
whatItDoes: Capecitabine becomes active only after your body converts it.
Enzymes in the liver and in tumor cells change it into fluorouracil, the active medicine.
Fluorouracil competes with the building blocks cells normally use to make DNA, RNA, and proteins.
That interference stops fast-dividing cancer cells from multiplying, which is why capecitabine treats cancer.
Approved uses include colon and rectal cancer, breast cancer that has spread, stomach and food-pipe cancer, and pancreatic cancer.
howPeopleUseIt: It is a tablet, not an intravenous drip, so most treatment happens at home.
The label says to swallow tablets whole with water within 30 minutes after a meal.
The label also says not to chew, cut, or crush them.
Most label regimens use 14 days of tablets followed by a rest period, repeated in 21-day cycles.
The label describes capecitabine as a hazardous drug with special handling and disposal rules.
It is heavily researched: a September 2026 ClinicalTrials.gov search found 2,871 registered studies mentioning it.

commonSideEffects: Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting are common, and diarrhea can be severe.
Hand-foot syndrome is common: the palms and soles turn red, sore, swollen, or peeling.
Mouth sores, stomach pain, tiredness, and loss of appetite are also reported.
Blood counts can drop, so the label recommends checking blood counts before each cycle.
The label reports raised bilirubin, a liver blood test, in many people taking capecitabine.
seriousSigns: The label's boxed warning says people born with complete DPD deficiency can have severe or fatal reactions.
DPD is an enzyme that breaks down fluorouracil, and some people have too little of it.
The label notes serious reactions can still happen even when no DPYD variant is found.
Heart problems including heart attack, chest pain, rhythm changes, and heart failure have been reported.
Serious skin reactions called Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis can occur and may be fatal.
Serious or fatal kidney failure has been reported, sometimes after dehydration from vomiting or diarrhea.
Myelosuppression, meaning the bone marrow makes fewer blood cells, can occur during treatment.
Bleeding, including death, is reported when capecitabine is combined with warfarin-type blood thinners.
whoShouldAvoid: The label says not to use it after a severe allergic reaction to fluorouracil or capecitabine.
It should also be avoided in people with DPYD variants that cause complete DPD deficiency.
The label advises women not to breastfeed during treatment and for one week after the last dose.
The label says capecitabine can harm a fetus and advises using effective contraception during treatment.
A safe dose has not been established for people with severely reduced kidney function.
It is not established for children; the label reports studies in 56 children with gliomas that did not show benefit.

interactions: Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonist blood thinners raise bleeding risk, so the label says to check INR often.
Allopurinol: the label says to avoid combining it, because it may reduce capecitabine's active breakdown products.
Leucovorin, folic acid, and folate products raise fluorouracil levels and toxicity, according to the label.
Phenytoin levels may rise, so the label says to monitor them and adjust the phenytoin dose.
Drugs processed by the liver enzyme CYP2C9, such as some blood thinners and diabetes drugs, reach higher levels.
Kidney-toxic drugs such as platinum chemotherapy, irinotecan, methotrexate, and IV bisphosphonates may add kidney risk.
An aluminum or magnesium antacid slightly raised capecitabine blood levels in a label study.
pregnancyAndChildren: Animal studies found capecitabine caused death and malformation in developing fetuses. The label says it can harm a human fetus, but human pregnancy data is limited. The label advises against breastfeeding during treatment and for one week after the last dose. Capecitabine is not approved for children. The label says safety and effectiveness have not been established, and lab abnormalities were more common in the children studied than in adults.
whatWeDoNotKnow: No source I read compares how people feel on capecitabine versus intravenous fluorouracil.
The label says tests for DPYD variants vary in accuracy and design, and that no FDA-authorized test existed when it was written.
The label says the effect of severe liver impairment on capecitabine is unknown.
It is unknown whether capecitabine passes into human breast milk.
The LiverTox chapter on capecitabine could not be read, so liver-injury detail here comes only from the drug label.
Nothing here covers cost, availability, or what a treatment course is like day to day.

gaps: NCCIH has no page for capecitabine: the requested URL returned a 404 not-found error, so NCCIH contributed nothing.
The LiverTox capecitabine chapter (NIDDK) was unreachable. Three URL forms were tried and all were stopped by a browser-verification page, so no independent liver-injury assessment could be grounded.
The PubChem human-readable compound page requires JavaScript and returned no content; only PubChem's structured data service was usable.
The NCI Drug Dictionary definition page rendered as an empty shell, so the NCI drug summary page was used instead.
MedlinePlus drug monographs were deliberately not fetched, cited, or used, because that content is copyrighted by ASHP.
No source read here compares capecitabine with intravenous fluorouracil for quality of life or convenience.
No grounded information was found on cost, supply, or the everyday experience of a treatment course.
The label's own statement is that the effect of severe hepatic impairment on capecitabine is unknown; that gap is reported rather than filled.
summary: This record covers what capecitabine is, how the body turns it into fluorouracil, its approved cancer uses, its common and serious side effects, its key interactions, and its pregnancy and children status, all grounded in the FDA label plus NCI, DailyMed, PubChem, and ClinicalTrials.gov.
